name: Anthralin (dithranol)

lead: Anthralin (dithranol) is a topical ointment mainly used for psoriasis that is also discussed for alopecia areata, the autoimmune patchy hair loss. People apply it to bald spots hoping for hair to regrow.

It irritates the skin, which is thought to shift the local immune response around the follicles, and it is reported to build up in mitochondria and slow cell division. A 2013 review reported tentative evidence of benefit for alopecia areata. It is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

paras: It comes as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%, applied to bald patches under clinician direction, often for a limited contact time before washing off. Regrowth, where it occurs, is judged over weeks to months.

Burning and irritation are reported, along with temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin and permanent staining of clothes and bathroom fixtures. In the UK it is a Pharmacy medicine, and it is used under clinician direction.

angle.text: Anthralin is a psoriasis ointment that people apply to bald spots of alopecia areata hoping for regrowth. It irritates the skin and shifts the local immune response, and a 2013 review reported tentative benefit; it is not a pattern-baldness treatment.

lead: Anthralin, also called dithranol, is a synthetic topical compound from the hydroxyanthrone and anthracene family, supplied as creams, ointments or pastes in strengths from roughly 0.1% to 2%. Its main established medical use is plaque psoriasis [1][2]. In hair-related contexts it is discussed as a topical irritant treatment for alopecia areata, an autoimmune patchy hair-loss condition.

The English Wikipedia article notes only tentative evidence that it may help alopecia areata, citing a 2013 review [1]. Documented effects include burning, irritation and temporary brown-to-purple staining of skin, and permanent staining of fabrics and bathroom fixtures [1].

paras: Anthralin is used on the skin for psoriasis. Wikipedia describes it as slower acting than topical steroids, usually taking several weeks, but without rebound flares after stopping; it is not used on the face or genitals [1]. American Academy of Dermatology guidelines on topical therapies for psoriasis place such agents among treatments that generally have a high efficacy-to-safety ratio for limited disease [2].

For alopecia areata, the idea behind irritant therapies such as anthralin is that provoking mild local skin irritation may change the immune activity around hair follicles. Wikipedia states that evidence for benefit is tentative and cites a 2013 review [1].

Reported effects include burning and irritation, which can be reduced by beginning with weaker preparations and increasing gradually. The compound can leave yellow-brown to purple temporary staining on skin and permanently stain clothing, shower curtains and ceramic sinks [1]. Surrounding skin is sometimes protected with soft paraffin [1].

The mechanism in psoriasis is not fully understood. It is reported to accumulate in mitochondria and may generate free radicals that disrupt cellular energy and DNA replication, slowing excess cell division; anti-inflammatory effects have also been reported [1].

Wikipedia summarises a 2013 review as showing tentative evidence of benefit in alopecia areata [1]. This article has not identified individual trials to report. Guidelines for psoriasis topical therapy discuss anthralin within that condition [2].
